title: Getting Past "I Tried That. It Doesn't Work."
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart reframes the familiar resistant phrase 'I tried that. It doesn't work.' as productive diagnostic information rather than a conversation-ending declaration. He connects the phrase to the Effort/Efficacy Doom Loop framework, reading it as a motivation signal that points to where someone is stuck. Three diagnostic categories emerge: the effort itself may have been ineffective, the person's definition of success may be misaligned with the strategy's actual purpose, or unexamined third variables may be at play. Stuart advocates for curiosity as the correct teacher response to this kind of statement — turning setback into an invitation to investigate rather than an occasion for frustration. The article ties this approach to Strategy #9 in The Will to Learn, 'Unpacking Outcomes, Good or Bad,' which cultivates accurate attribution of results to their actual causes and thereby sustains both motivation and professional development.
points: 'I tried that. It doesn't work.' is Effort/Efficacy language — a signal that someone is stuck in the Doom Loop and needs help directing their mind toward the specifics of what went wrong.
Three diagnostic categories for unpacking any 'it didn't work': the effort put forth was actually ineffective, the definition of success was misaligned, or unrecognized third variables were at play.
The key investigative question to cultivate is 'Hmm — I wonder why?' — a shift from discouragement to curiosity that makes failure generative rather than terminal.
Helping learners define success wisely — not as overnight transformation or a grade, but as mastery and accurate attribution — is itself a core motivational strategy.
Curiosity about setbacks keeps teaching alive; without it, each failure compounds into a heavier professional burden rather than a useful data point.
quotes: Once in a while, I'll hear a student or a teacher say this when I bring up a strategy: "I tried that. It doesn't work." On its face, this is a frustrating thing for a teacher to hear. After all, the person seems to have come to the conclusion that there's nothing more to learn here.

if you dig deeper, this is actually a really helpful communication. The person is saying, "Hey, I've got a motivation problem. The effort didn't pay off. I can't be successful doing that." It's Effort/Efficacy language. The person is stuck somewhere within the Effort/Efficacy Doom Loop.

It could be that the effort put forth — "I tried that" — was ineffective. Maybe a teacher attempted a Moment of Genuine Connection (MGC), for example, but it was rote, unfeeling, or disingenuous. Maybe a student studied with self-quizzing, but they were checking their phone pings throughout the study session.

It could be that they have an unhelpful definition of success. What does "it didn't work" mean? If they were hoping that an MGC was going to transform student behaviors overnight, that's a problem. That's not what MGCs do.
When we're not curious about setbacks, the work gets to be a heavy load on our souls. But when we ARE curious, watch out — even failure can be fun and generative.

It's this kind of thinking that undergirds the whole idea of "Unpacking Outcomes, Good or Bad" (Strategy #9 in The Will to Learn). The strategy helps with Five Key Belief cultivation (in teachers or students) because it gets us curious about results — which do matter! — and helps us more accurately attribute those results to their true causes.
